name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,742

clue.text: A jolly old fellow in Battle

blocks.note: taken as written
a jolly is old slang for a Royal Marine, abbreviated RM
old means advanced in years
a don is a university fellow

explanation.surface: A cheerful elderly man is caught up in the middle of a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jolly old fellow' reads as one merry man, but it splits three ways: jolly (Royal Marine), old, fellow. ARMAGEDDON is the prophesied final battle.
explanation.definitionFit: Armageddon names the biblical site of the last great conflict, and by extension any catastrophic, decisive war.

clue.text: Foremost of shorts-wearers doesn't own trousers

indicators.note: foremost means frontmost, so only the opening letter of the next word is kept

blocks.note: the opening letter of the hyphenated word
to lack something is not to have it

explanation.surface: The leading shorts-wearer has no long trousers in the wardrobe.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sets shorts against trousers, which neatly hides that the whole last word is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Slacks are casual long trousers, a straightforward synonym for the garment in everyday clothing vocabulary.

clue.text: Criminal has dame overcome with guilt

indicators.note: something criminal is bent or crooked, so the letters that follow are twisted out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lady who has committed a crime is racked with remorse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' looks like a noun describing the dame, but it is the signal to rearrange the next two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling ashamed means being filled with embarrassment and remorse about one's own wrongdoing.

clue.text: Trees in fresco needing to be touched up

indicators.note: a painting that needs touching up must be reworked, so the letters are remade in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A wall painting of a woodland scene needs restoring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' reads as a placing word, putting the trees inside the fresco, but it is part of the letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Conifers are cone-bearing trees such as pines, firs and spruces, so they are one kind of tree.

clue.text: Talk about start of affair? It's a long story!

indicators.note: about can mean turned round, as in an about-turn, so the word runs backwards
the start of a word is its opening letter, which is all that is kept

blocks.note: to gas is to chatter idly
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Gossiping about how an affair began turns into a lengthy tale.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation 'It's a long story!' sounds like a weary aside but is the definition in full.
explanation.definitionFit: A saga is a lengthy narrative, originally an Icelandic heroic tale, now any long drawn-out account of events.

clue.text: Man covering R&B and bit of soul rocks

indicators.note: to cover something is to wrap around it, so one piece goes outside another
a bit of a word is a small piece, here just its opening letter

blocks.note: a man is a male
the ampersand is dropped, leaving the two letters
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A singer doing R&B covers with a touch of soul really rocks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Covering' and 'rocks' read as music talk, a cover version that rocks; covering is the container signal and rocks is the definition, as a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Marbles are pieces of polished stone, and rocks can mean stones, so the plural nouns correspond.

clue.text: Hoskins is getting train (north-bound) for foreign resort

indicators.note: in a down entry heading north means travelling upwards, so the letters read bottom to top

blocks.note: Hoskins is the setter, so 'Hoskins is' becomes I'm
to train a gun on something is to aim it

explanation.surface: The setter is catching a northbound train to go on a holiday abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often name themselves in clues, so 'Hoskins' stands for I or ME. Train is a verb here, as in training a camera on someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Miami is a Florida beach city, a holiday destination that lies overseas from the British setter's viewpoint.

clue.text: Primate called on phone at centre

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letter, the only one kept
in an across entry, one thing on another comes after it, so the piece it attaches to is written second

blocks.note: the middle letter of a five-letter word
rang means telephoned

explanation.surface: An ape gets a phone call at the zoo's primate centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Called on phone' reads as one phrase meaning rang, but the phone belongs to the letter selection; 'on' places the call after that letter in an across entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Orang is a short form of orangutan, the great ape of Borneo and Sumatra, which is a primate.

clue.text: Strong wind engulfing priest around region abroad

indicators.note: turned around means facing the other way, so the word runs backwards
to engulf is to swallow up, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: a gale is a strong wind
Eli is the Old Testament priest who raised Samuel, a crossword staple

explanation.surface: A gale sweeps a clergyman off his feet somewhere overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' looks like it goes with 'region', but it reverses the priest before the wind swallows him.
explanation.definitionFit: Galilee is a historic area of northern Israel, a territory in another country from the setter's viewpoint.

clue.text: Sparkling wine woodworker picked up

indicators.note: to pick up is to catch by ear, so the word is judged by how it is heard

blocks.note: a carver shapes wood; in a non-rhotic British accent it matches the wine

explanation.surface: A carpenter takes a bottle of fizz off the shelf.
explanation.walkthrough: The match relies on a British accent that drops the R in carver.
explanation.definitionFit: Cava is a Spanish white wine made fizzy by the traditional method, like champagne.

clue.text: Being philanthropic is a real bitch, sadly

indicators.note: sadly suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters are left in a mess

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles that giving to good causes is, unfortunately, a real pain.
explanation.walkthrough: The complaint is ironic since the answer is generous; 'Being philanthropic' is read as an adjective phrase, as in 'being kind'.
explanation.definitionFit: A philanthropic person gives generously to those in need, which is what a charitable person does.

clue.text: Landlord in Cleese remake

indicators.note: a remake is a new version of an old work, so the letters are made again in another order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; John Cleese is the Fawlty Towers comic

explanation.surface: A hotel keeper appears in a remake of a John Cleese comedy, a nod to Fawlty Towers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' seems to place the landlord in the film, but its letters join the name to be rearranged. In Britain a landlord is also the person who runs a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A British pub landlord holds the licence to sell alcohol, so is officially the licensee of the premises.

clue.text: Former Tory leader Bowles regularly praises

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter is kept
at regular intervals, so every second letter is kept

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner or holder
the opening letter of the word
second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A one-time Conservative leader named Bowles is full of praise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Former Tory leader' reads as one job title, but it is three instructions. Camilla Bowles was never a party leader; the name only supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To extol someone is to commend them enthusiastically, a formal verb matching praises in the third person.

clue.text: Contest rent with amount written in error

indicators.note: something written wrongly has its letters in the wrong order, so they must be rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tenant disputes a rent bill on which the wrong sum was entered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contest' reads as a verb, to challenge the rent, but the definition is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A tournament is a series of games or matches between competitors, a competitive event just like a contest.

clue.text: Drink in the morning is something non-pro players do

blocks.note: a.m. marks the hours before noon
a dram is a small measure of spirits, especially whisky

explanation.surface: Amateur sportsmen are known for having a morning tipple.
explanation.walkthrough: The drink is written first but sits second: read it as 'drink, with the morning in front'. Am-dram is British shorthand for amateur dramatics, local theatre groups.
explanation.definitionFit: Amateur actors put on plays unpaid, and players can mean actors, so their hobby is amateur dramatics.

clue.text: A party, but avoiding contact with others

blocks.note: taken as written
an informal get-together, such as a club's evening do

explanation.surface: Someone goes to a party yet keeps away from everyone there.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'but' is a genuine contrast in the surface, since a party is sociable; the answer is its opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: An asocial person shuns company and interaction, preferring to keep themselves apart from other people.

clue.text: Having stolen ball, Athletic supporters in scrape

indicators.note: a thief who has stolen something holds it, so one piece is taken inside another

blocks.note: A is a standard abbreviation for Athletic in football club names
bras are supportive underwear
taken as written
a ball is round, like the letter O

explanation.surface: After a player nicks the ball, Athletic fans find themselves in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporters' and 'Athletic' paint football fans; supporters are underwear here. 'In scrape' looks like an idiom for trouble, but scrape is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An abrasion is a graze where skin has been rubbed or scraped away, so the nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Fancy fool meeting with you and your setter

blocks.note: an ass is a foolish person
U stands for you in text speak
the setter refers to himself as me

explanation.surface: An idiot hopes to get together with the solver and the setter.
explanation.walkthrough: The parts spell the old saying that to assume makes an ass of you and me. 'Fancy' is a verb meaning suppose, as in 'I fancy it will rain'.
explanation.definitionFit: To fancy something can mean to believe or imagine it without proof, which is to take it for granted.

clue.text: Sort of rifle nurse found on battleground

blocks.note: EN is an Enrolled Nurse
a field of battle is where fighting takes place

explanation.surface: A medic is discovered on the battlefield with a gun of some kind.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'found on' puts the nurse above the field. The Lee-Enfield was the standard British army rifle for decades.
explanation.definitionFit: Enfield rifles, named after the Royal Small Arms Factory in north London, are a type of military firearm.

clue.text: German article about private's depressing experience

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word goes around another

blocks.note: der is the masculine definite article in German
one's own is private, belonging to oneself alone

explanation.surface: A German newspaper piece describes a common soldier's miserable time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Private' suggests an army private; it is an adjective, as in 'my own room'.
explanation.definitionFit: A downer is informal for something that makes you feel low, a dispiriting event or bleak situation.

clue.text: Tag prison's given to backsliding English chap

indicators.note: sliding backwards means going the opposite way, so the letters run right to left

blocks.note: nick is British slang for a prison or police station
E is the standard abbreviation for English
a chap is a man

explanation.surface: An electronic tag in prison is fitted to an Englishman who has reoffended.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tag' reads as the offender's ankle tag, but it means a label or name.
explanation.definitionFit: A tag can be an informal label or name someone is known by, which is a familiar alternative name.

clue.text: Old leader could be usurper, you say?

indicators.note: what you say is spoken, so the word is judged by its sound

blocks.note: a usurper seizes power, so is a seizer

explanation.surface: Someone wonders aloud whether an ancient ruler was really an illegitimate one.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke fits history: Julius Caesar did grab power in Rome, so the old leader really was a seizer.
explanation.definitionFit: Julius Caesar was the Roman general and dictator, and the name became a title for later emperors.

clue.text: Car space entered by Ford model (after reversing)

indicators.note: something entered has a thing go inside it, so one piece sits within another
reversing means backing up, so the result is read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: room means space
the Model T was Ford's famous early car

explanation.surface: A Ford backs into a parking space.
explanation.walkthrough: Reversing the space first and then inserting the letter gives the same result as reversing afterwards, since the letter sits in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Motor is an old-fashioned or informal British word for an automobile, as in motor car.

clue.text: Contemptuous teacher I have on flipping side ... mostly

indicators.note: to flip something is to turn it over, so the word runs backwards
mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is removed

blocks.note: the word turned round
pupils address a female teacher as Miss
the contraction I've

explanation.surface: A scornful teacher mutters about her flipping job, more or less.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild British swear word, but it turns the word round; the shortened piece sits in front, since 'on' places the others after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Being dismissive means treating something as unworthy of consideration, showing disdain or scorn for it.

clue.text: Bang your head mildly on shell housing at the front

indicators.note: the front of each word is its opening letter, so only those are kept

blocks.note: the opening letters of four words

explanation.surface: Someone at a gig knocks their head gently against the shell of a building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Housing' feels like a container signal but is only a source word. Moshing is the rough dancing at rock gigs where people headbang.
explanation.definitionFit: To mosh is to dance violently at a rock or metal concert, which often involves headbanging.

clue.text: West opened with lead of trumps for partner

indicators.note: the lead is what goes first, so only the opening letter is kept
something opened up has a gap made in it for another piece to fill

blocks.note: Mae West was the Hollywood actress
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: At bridge, West leads a trump to help his partner.
explanation.walkthrough: The bridge terms (West, lead, trumps, partner) are a smokescreen; West is the actress's surname, standing for her first name.
explanation.definitionFit: A mate is a companion or spouse, and a bridge player sits opposite their teammate called a partner.

clue.text: Girl, head of Openbank, that might hold bit of stock

definitions.text: that might hold bit of stock

indicators.note: the head is the top, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: a lass is a girl
the opening letter of the bank's name

explanation.surface: A young woman running an online bank might own some shares.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stock' suggests shares, but it is livestock: a lasso catches and holds a steer.
explanation.definitionFit: A cowboy's rope with a running noose is thrown to catch and restrain cattle or horses, so it holds livestock.

clue.text: Large person bringing home bacon for schoolboy?

blocks.note: L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
to bring home the bacon is to earn a living

explanation.surface: A big breadwinner is being likened to a pupil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bringing home the bacon' is an idiom for earning money. The question mark flags that a schoolboy is only one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A schoolboy is a pupil still being taught, one instance of someone acquiring knowledge or skills.
